newsitem.title: UK: UK gilts this week - spotlight on labour market.
newsitem.headline: UK gilts this week - spotlight on labour market.

text.p: UK gilts should get a respite from political wrangling this week as the spotlight shifts to the labour market, where benign earnings data are seen adding to evidence that UK inflation pressures remain dormant.
Add to that an expected sharp drop in the government borrowing requirement for September and gilts should hold their ground, if not outperform some non-core European markets.
"In the absence of other news I expect gilts to tighten mildly on switching out of other European peripherals," said Mark Capleton, international bond strategist at BZW.
Gilts kicked off the week in a consolidation mood after emerging relatively unscathed from three consecutive weeks of political party conferences.
With the focus back on economic data, Wednesday's unemployment, earnings and PSBR (government borrowing requirement) figures are seen as pivotal.

Economists expect unemployment, which has fallen at an average monthly rate of some 17,000 over the last six months, to fall by another 20,000 in September, tightening the labour market another notch.
But with average earnings growth steady at 3.75 percent since February, and forecast to have stuck at this level again in August, inflationary pressures remain subdued.
"The general outlook for inflation is still benign for the time being," said Steve Scott, gilts analyst at Kleinwort Benson. "I don't think gilts will be too upset by the labour market figures."
Ciaran Barr, economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said average earnings growth should edge up to around 4.0 percent by year-end before rising more sharply in 1997.
"While there is a reasonable chance that earnings will edge up this month, we believe the balance of probability favours underlying earnings remaining unchanged at 3.75 percent in August," he added.

The PSBR is seen dropping to 2.7 billion stg in September from 4.5 billion in August, reinforcing expectations that the government may meet its target of a 27 billion stg deficit in the current financial year.
"The authorites are well up with the rate of funding this year so that's not a worry at the moment...in fact, it's in line to fractionally ahead," said Scott.
Some rebound in VAT receipts, further evidence of control of public spending and privatisation receipts of around one billion sterling are all seen keeping a lid on borrowing needs.
Analysts said the short-term outlook for the gilt/Bund 10-year spread was difficult to call at current levels.
"It's a bit tricky at the moment," said Scott. "We've got it closing...to 150 basis points by the end of the year and 140 by March 1997, so there's a gradual closing in the longer term."
But with the spread having narrowed by up to 30 basis points in the last three weeks, the scope for further near-term tightening appears limited.
BZW's Capleton said gilts may get a boost this week as doubts emerge about the ability of "peripheral" European countries to make the Maastricht grade.

"There's lots of chat about Ecofin meetings where perhaps there are doubts about the likely convergence of fundamentals of countries like Italy and Spain," he said, adding that this may spark some profit-taking in those markets.
Broad money supply data for September, due on Friday, are expected to show a slight rise in year-on year growth to 9.6 percent from 9.4 percent in August.
But with M4 growth running at or above the top of the government's three to nine percent monitoring range for almost a year, the data are not expected to alarm the market.
